title: The Educated Barbarian: Hagakure analysis (part. 19)
summary: NH begins Hagakure book three, his least favourite because it is mostly anecdotes, and draws lessons on categorising people, healthy versus unhealthy hierarchies, extreme samurai devotion, the contradictions in absolute codes, and luck. He concludes that luck can't be controlled, so focus on preparation and action.
claims: Book three is NH's least favourite of the Hagakure: long anecdotes leave him less room to extrapolate than short maxims like those in The Book of Five Rings
Hagakure sorts retainers by how fast they understand and how fast they execute, an early version of managers' type A and type B labels
Avoid thinking of people in broad categories; it breeds stereotypes, disappointment and eventually disgust for humanity, which hurts you first
A healthy hierarchy is one where those at the bottom see those at the top as having earned it; unfair hierarchies eventually collapse
Humans always exist within hierarchies, more complex and volatile than animals', and your status changes from group to group
Most people today aren't devoted enough even to fight for their own life, let alone for family; most err toward doing nothing
Absolute teachings lead to absolute contradictions; living by a code requires flexibility and interpretation case by case
Surviving to fight again can outweigh preserving perceived honour; staying alive is part of loyalty
Using presence to defuse a fight that would get everyone killed is bravery, not cowardice
Luck plays a huge role in life and can't be systematised; humans are born unequal and true equality is impossible
You can't control luck, fate or destiny, so don't waste time on them; control your preparedness and act when you can
The Hagakure's anecdotes add nuance by showing how to apply its rules in real situations
